title: GlanceAR: Repurposing Phone Sensors via Low-Cost Reflectors for Always-On Obstacle Awareness
summary: Smartphone use while walking reduces environmental awareness and can lead to accidents and injury, yet existing obstacle-awareness systems remain unadopted because they require users to hold the phone upright and aimed forward, conflicting with how people actually hold their devices. We introduce GlanceAR, an always-on mobile obstacle-awareness system designed for natural phone-holding postures. GlanceAR utilizes a low-cost passive mirror attachment to redirect the phone's rear LiDAR and RGB camera forward without additional electronic components. In a within-subjects study with N=11 participants navigating indoor and outdoor obstacle courses while engaged in a primary on-phone task, we evaluated three sensing configurations: GlanceAR, a LiDAR-only variant for privacy, and an attachment-free ultra-wide camera baseline. Our findings reveal trade-offs among sensing fidelity, obstacle cue design, and social acceptability, and surface insights around AI complacency and the tension between on-screen task focus and physical safety.

AI.tldr: GlanceAR is an always-on smartphone obstacle-awareness system that uses a passive mirror attachment to redirect rear-facing LiDAR and RGB sensing forward, enabling obstacle detection during natural phone use. A study with 11 participants compared GlanceAR, a privacy-preserving LiDAR-only version, and an attachment-free ultra-wide-camera baseline, revealing trade-offs among sensing performance, cue design, privacy, social acceptability, and user reliance.
AI.motivation: Existing smartphone obstacle-awareness systems are difficult to adopt because they assume users hold the phone upright and point it forward, which conflicts with natural phone-holding behavior during walking. The paper addresses the safety risks of reduced environmental awareness while using a phone and seeks a practical, low-cost, always-on solution that does not require additional electronic hardware.
AI.method: The authors developed GlanceAR, which uses a passive mirror attachment to redirect the smartphone's rear LiDAR and RGB camera toward the user's forward path. They conducted a within-subjects study with 11 participants navigating indoor and outdoor obstacle courses while performing a primary task on the phone. Three configurations were compared: the full GlanceAR system, a LiDAR-only privacy-oriented variant, and an attachment-free ultra-wide-camera baseline. The evaluation examined sensing fidelity, obstacle-alert cue design, privacy, social acceptability, and issues related to user reliance on automated assistance.
AI.result: The study identified trade-offs between sensing fidelity and privacy, as well as between different obstacle-cue designs and social acceptability. The results also highlighted potential AI complacency, in which users may over-rely on system alerts, and a conflict between maintaining attention on the on-screen task and responding safely to the physical environment. The abstract does not report quantitative performance metrics or statistical results.
AI.conclusion: A passive optical attachment can support forward obstacle awareness while allowing users to hold smartphones naturally, offering a potentially more adoptable alternative to systems requiring a forward-facing phone posture. However, successful deployment requires careful balancing of detection capability, privacy, unobtrusive cue design, social acceptability, and safeguards against over-reliance on automated warnings.

title: Whale You Go Green? Immediate and Longitudinal Effects of Embodied Conversational AI Avatars on Sustainable Behavioral Tendencies and Pro-Environmental Attitudes
summary: Embodied conversational AI can be persuasive, but can it motivate people to develop sustainable behavioral tendencies and increase pro-environmental attitudes? We conducted a randomized experiment (N = 576) comparing four embodied avatars--a beluga whale, Greta Thunberg, Emma Watson, and a generic human--with a text chatbot and no-intervention control. All embodied conditions increased immediate sustainable product selection relative to the control (beta = .401-.609, all q <= .0126) and chatbot (beta = .398-.604, all q <= .007), without differing significantly from one another. Only the Beluga condition increased immediate pro-environmental attitudes relative to the control after correction. Among 287 returners assessed two months later, following an intermediate assigned-condition session, Beluga also showed significantly higher pre-booster sustainable product choice compared to the control (beta = .657, q = .0176). Although it did not significantly outperform other embodied agents, these findings establish the immediate potential of nonhuman embodied avatar interfaces as a promising direction for memorable environmental interventions.

AI.tldr: A randomized experiment found that embodied conversational agents—especially a beluga whale avatar—can immediately improve sustainable product choices compared with a text chatbot or no intervention. Evidence for lasting effects was limited but suggested a possible advantage for the beluga condition after two months.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses whether embodied conversational AI can move beyond short-term persuasion to encourage sustainable behavioral tendencies and strengthen pro-environmental attitudes. It also examines whether avatar identity, including a nonhuman agent, affects intervention effectiveness relative to text-only interaction and no intervention.
AI.method: The study randomly assigned 576 participants to six conditions: four embodied avatars (a beluga whale, Greta Thunberg, Emma Watson, and a generic human), a text chatbot, or a no-intervention control. Outcomes included immediate sustainable product selection and pro-environmental attitudes. A subset of 287 participants returned two months later and completed an intermediate assigned-condition session before a pre-booster behavioral assessment. Effects were evaluated using beta coefficients and multiplicity-adjusted q-values.
AI.result: All embodied-avatar conditions significantly increased immediate sustainable product selection relative to both the no-intervention control (β = .401–.609; all q ≤ .0126) and the text chatbot (β = .398–.604; all q ≤ .007). The embodied avatars did not significantly differ from one another on this outcome. Only the beluga condition significantly improved immediate pro-environmental attitudes relative to the control after correction. At the two-month assessment, the beluga condition produced higher pre-booster sustainable product choice than the control (β = .657, q = .0176), although it did not significantly outperform the other embodied agents.
AI.conclusion: Embodied conversational interfaces appear to have strong immediate potential for promoting sustainable choices, with performance superior to text-based and inactive controls. The beluga avatar provides preliminary evidence that a nonhuman agent may support attitude change and longer-term behavioral persistence, but the lack of consistent differences among embodied agents and the reduced follow-up sample mean that claims about durable or avatar-specific effects should remain cautious.

title: The As-If Machine: Personalized counterfactuals make distant policy risks feel close
summary: Life experiences can shape policy attitudes, but we only live one life. Citizens may therefore fail to support policies addressing risks they have never personally experienced. Narratives can make such risks immediate and personal, but personalized stories remain difficult to produce at scale. Here we ask whether AI can make distant scenarios feel concrete by simulating a participant's life as if that scenario occurred. We present the As-If Machine (AIM), a multi-agent system through which people co-write personalized counterfactual narratives---stories about their own lives under different policy futures. In two pre-registered and quota-matched experiments on science funding (N=1,007) and satellite cybersecurity (N=894), we compared AIM with two controls: reading an expert-written vignette on the same topic and co-writing with AIM about an unrelated topic. AIM increased psychological closeness---how close a risk feels to the self---by nearly identical margins in the two domains (0.36 and 0.38 standard deviations (SDs) against the vignette, 0.80 and 0.90 against unrelated writing). AIM increased psychological closeness even among participants with unfavorable views of AI. For policy attitudes, AIM's effects were 0.16 SDs against the vignette and 0.10 SDs (n.s.) against unrelated writing for science funding; the corresponding effects for satellite cybersecurity were 0.54 and 0.67 SDs. Across 23,496 human-AI autocomplete interactions, participants and the system played distinct roles: AIM supplied concrete detail that grounded the scenario, and participants supplied first-person perspective and emotion. Co-writing with the As-If Machine makes distant policy risks feel close.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether a multi-agent AI system can make unfamiliar policy risks feel personally relevant by helping people co-write counterfactual stories about their own lives. Across two preregistered experiments, the As-If Machine increased psychological closeness in both science funding and satellite cybersecurity, with policy-attitude effects that were stronger and more consistent for satellite cybersecurity than for science funding.
AI.motivation: People often form policy attitudes from personal experience, but they cannot directly experience every societal risk. Conventional expert-written narratives may be less personally engaging, and producing individualized narratives at scale is difficult. The study therefore asks whether AI-generated, personalized counterfactual narratives can make distant risks feel more immediate and influence policy attitudes.
AI.method: The authors introduced the As-If Machine (AIM), a multi-agent system that collaborates with participants to write narratives about their own lives under hypothetical policy futures. Two preregistered, quota-matched experiments examined science funding (N=1,007) and satellite cybersecurity (N=894). Participants were assigned to AIM, an expert-written vignette control, or AIM co-writing about an unrelated topic. Outcomes included psychological closeness to the risk and policy attitudes. The authors also analyzed 23,496 human-AI autocomplete interactions to characterize each side’s contribution.
AI.result: AIM increased psychological closeness relative to expert vignettes by 0.36 SDs in the science-funding study and 0.38 SDs in the satellite-cybersecurity study; effects relative to unrelated writing were 0.80 and 0.90 SDs. These effects persisted among participants who viewed AI unfavorably. Policy-attitude effects relative to the vignette were 0.16 SDs for science funding and 0.54 SDs for satellite cybersecurity; relative to unrelated writing, they were 0.10 SDs and 0.67 SDs, respectively. The science-funding effect against unrelated writing was not statistically significant. Interaction analysis indicated that AIM contributed concrete situational detail, while participants contributed first-person perspective and emotion.
AI.conclusion: Co-writing personalized counterfactual narratives with AIM can reliably increase the psychological closeness of unfamiliar policy risks. The evidence for changing policy attitudes is promising but domain-dependent: effects were modest or nonsignificant for science funding and substantially larger for satellite cybersecurity. The findings support AI-assisted narrative personalization as a scalable communication approach, while also suggesting that changes in perceived closeness do not automatically produce equally strong changes in policy preferences.

title: FlashScript: Compiling Recurring Agent Workflows into Reusable Neuro-Symbolic Programs
summary: Many agent tasks recur with new data or small changes, yet agents regenerate their reasoning and actions on each run, producing different results. Distilling a prior run into a skill helps the agent avoid earlier mistakes, but it still re-runs the full process each time, so runs can vary and incur that cost. We compile a successful agent run into a reusable neuro-symbolic program (NSP) with a set of guidelines we call FlashScript. Actions and data transformations become code, instance-specific values become parameters, and decisions that need model judgment become LLM calls. We identify three layers where these calls belong and three techniques that replace most of them with code. The compilation does not remove nondeterminism; it localizes it, so the deterministic program and its neural calls can be reviewed and tested separately. Across 120 WorkBench analytics tasks with Claude Haiku 4.5, the NSPs were correct and made identical tool calls on every run, using about 70 times fewer input tokens and a third of the runtime of a skill-guided agent whose runs were inconsistent. In a composite version of the tasks, the skill-guided agent's accuracy fell to 23%, and its output inconsistency increased, while the NSPs remained correct and identical across all runs. The NSPs successfully generalized to all 108 unseen instances of the same templates. Our findings suggest that NSPs from agent trajectories can be considered cumulative software assets for end-users to test, maintain, and reuse in their recurring workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes compiling successful agent trajectories into reusable neuro-symbolic programs (NSPs), called FlashScript, that convert repeatable actions and data transformations into deterministic code while retaining LLM calls only for judgment-dependent decisions. Across 120 WorkBench analytics tasks, these NSPs were correct, repeatable, far more token-efficient, and faster than skill-guided agents, and they generalized to 108 unseen instances.
AI.motivation: Recurring agent tasks are often rerun on new data or with minor variations. Conventional agents regenerate the entire reasoning-and-action process, causing unnecessary cost, nondeterministic outputs, and repeated mistakes. Although skills can guide future runs, they do not eliminate full re-execution or inconsistency. The paper addresses the need to turn successful trajectories into inspectable, maintainable, and reusable workflow assets.
AI.method: The authors compile a successful agent run into a neuro-symbolic program using FlashScript guidelines. Actions and data transformations are represented as code, instance-specific values are parameterized, and decisions requiring semantic or contextual judgment remain as LLM calls. The method organizes these calls into three layers and introduces three techniques for replacing most calls with deterministic code. This design localizes, rather than eliminates, nondeterminism, allowing the program and neural components to be tested and reviewed separately. Evaluation compares NSPs with skill-guided agents on 120 WorkBench analytics tasks, composite task settings, and 108 unseen instances sharing the same templates.
AI.result: NSPs produced correct outputs and identical tool calls across repeated runs. They used approximately 70 times fewer input tokens and one-third of the runtime of skill-guided agents, whose runs were inconsistent. On composite tasks, skill-guided accuracy dropped to 23% and inconsistency increased, whereas NSPs remained correct and identical on every run. NSPs also generalized successfully to all 108 unseen instances.
AI.conclusion: Compiling agent trajectories into NSPs can transform one successful execution into a cumulative software asset. By encoding stable workflow logic as deterministic code and isolating the remaining neural decisions, the approach improves reliability, efficiency, reproducibility, testability, and reuse in recurring end-user workflows.

title: Human-Aware Agentic Driving: Rethinking Driver State, Trust, and Intervention
summary: Agentic driving brings goal-directed reasoning, memory, tools, and adaptive interaction into automated vehicles. A vehicle can clarify a request, explain a maneuver, or prepare a driver to take control, then adapt its next action to the response. These capabilities make the vehicle an active participant in shaping the human behavior it observes. We examine how agentic interaction affects driver-state inference, trust and reliance, and human intervention in conditional automation. Established findings on attention, takeover prediction, trust-aware planning, and adaptive warnings provide useful foundations, but their applicability depends on how observations are elicited and how assistance changes the driving task. We distinguish what remains applicable, what changes under flexible interaction, and what remains unresolved across these three areas. The analysis identifies three research priorities: establishing the effects of interventions, jointly designing interaction and driving policies, and maintaining useful adaptation across repeated use and system changes. Progress should be measured through driver comprehension, appropriate reliance, and the ability to perform the required driving action in time.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how agentic interaction in conditional automated vehicles changes driver-state inference, trust and reliance, and human intervention. It synthesizes prior research, identifies which established findings remain valid or require revision, and proposes priorities for evaluating adaptive vehicle behavior.
AI.motivation: Conventional automated-driving research often treats the vehicle as a relatively fixed system that observes the driver and issues assistance. Agentic driving introduces goal-directed dialogue, memory, tools, clarification, explanations, and adaptive interaction, meaning the vehicle can actively shape the driver's attention, trust, reliance, and readiness to intervene. The paper is motivated by the need to reassess existing findings under these more flexible, interactive conditions and to define evaluation criteria that reflect safe human-vehicle cooperation.
AI.method: The paper presents a conceptual and analytical synthesis of established work on attention, takeover prediction, trust-aware planning, and adaptive warnings. It organizes the analysis around three topics—driver-state inference, trust and reliance, and human intervention—then examines how agentic interaction changes the observations available to the system and the driving task itself. It distinguishes conclusions that remain applicable, those requiring modification, and unresolved questions, and derives three research priorities: measuring intervention effects, jointly designing interaction and driving policies, and sustaining effective adaptation over repeated use and system changes.
AI.result: The analysis finds that prior results cannot be transferred directly to agentic vehicles because interaction may both reveal and alter driver state. Assistance, clarification, and explanations can affect attention, trust, reliance, and takeover readiness, creating feedback between system behavior and the behavior being inferred. The paper identifies unresolved issues concerning the causal effects of interventions, coordination between interaction policies and vehicle-control policies, and adaptation that remains useful as drivers and system configurations change. It proposes evaluating systems through driver comprehension, appropriate rather than excessive reliance, and timely ability to perform the required driving action.
AI.conclusion: Agentic driving requires a shift from passive driver monitoring toward designing and evaluating a coupled human-system interaction. Safe progress depends on understanding how the vehicle's interventions shape the driver, integrating interaction decisions with driving decisions, and preserving effective adaptation across time. Success should be judged by whether drivers understand the situation, rely on automation appropriately, and can complete necessary interventions within the available time.

title: InteractiveWorld: A Verifiable Human-Centric Environment for Building Better Interactive MLLM Assistants
summary: People have long dreamed of an assistant that is always there to guide them and remind what they forget, from new dishes to lost keys. Powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs), egocentric AI assistants on wearable devices are bringing this dream within reach: they see what the user sees and give instructions for user's physical work when necessary. However, testing such assistance is challenging and usually requires real people. The expensive and rare real interaction data leaves a key question unanswered: Can today's MLLMs truly help people in physical world? To answer this question, we propose InteractiveWorld, the first verifiable environment for closed-loop interaction between human and AI assistant. Unlike existing robot-centric simulators, InteractiveWorld lets the assistant guide a human agent who observes the scene, understands instructions, and acts independently. It thus realistically simulates how AI assistant collaborates with human: the assistant instructs, the human acts, and the environment executes actions and updates what they see next. Building on it, we introduce InteractiveBench, the first dynamic benchmark for egocentric AI assistants, with 120 multi-turn tasks across six categories. In each task, the assistant guides the human in real time, and every instruction shapes the outcome, which is scored by verifiable, state-based rewards. Experiments with 12 frontier MLLMs show they are still far from reliable assistants. Even the strongest model, Claude Fable 5.1, achieves at most 20% and 25% on long-horizon Guidance and Planning tasks, respectively. Overall, our work offers a verifiable platform and a rigorous evaluation set, laying a solid foundation for research on interactive MLLM assistants that truly help people in the physical world.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces InteractiveWorld, a verifiable closed-loop simulation environment, and InteractiveBench, a 120-task benchmark for evaluating egocentric multimodal AI assistants that guide human agents through physical-world tasks. Experiments across 12 frontier MLLMs show substantial limitations, especially on long-horizon guidance and planning.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of egocentric AI assistants rely heavily on costly and scarce real human interaction data or robot-centric simulators. These settings do not adequately test whether a multimodal large language model can provide reliable, real-time guidance to a person performing physical tasks. The paper addresses the need for a controllable, reproducible, and verifiable evaluation framework for human–AI collaboration in dynamic environments.
AI.method: The authors develop InteractiveWorld, a closed-loop environment in which an AI assistant observes an egocentric scene and issues instructions, while a human agent independently interprets and executes actions. The environment updates the scene after each action, allowing every instruction to influence subsequent states. On top of this environment, they construct InteractiveBench, comprising 120 multi-turn tasks spanning six categories. Performance is measured using verifiable state-based rewards. They evaluate 12 frontier multimodal large language models on the benchmark, focusing particularly on long-horizon guidance and planning.
AI.result: The evaluated MLLMs perform poorly overall and are not yet reliable physical-world assistants. The best reported model, Claude Fable 5.1, achieves no more than 20% on long-horizon Guidance tasks and 25% on Planning tasks. These results indicate difficulties with sustained interaction, action sequencing, state tracking, and reliable task completion.
AI.conclusion: InteractiveWorld and InteractiveBench provide a reproducible platform for evaluating interactive egocentric AI assistants without depending exclusively on costly real-user experiments. The findings show that current frontier MLLMs remain far from dependable assistance in physical environments, while the proposed framework establishes a foundation for improving and systematically studying interactive multimodal agents.

title: A spinal-inspired spiking neural network for continuous finger-joint kinematics estimation from high-density surface EMG
comment: 32 pages (25 pages of main text and 7 pages of supplementary material), 9 figures, 1 table
summary: Decoding simultaneous and proportional finger kinematics from high-density surface electromyography (HD sEMG) remains challenging. Although data-driven methods have shown promising performance for finger movement decoding, their limited physiological interpretability remains a relevant limitation. This study proposes and evaluates a spiking neural network (SNN) that incorporates spinal-inspired structures and mechanisms to predict multi-joint finger kinematics from HD sEMG signals. The spinal-inspired SNN includes a spike-encoding computational model with input-noise variability, a phenomenological representation of Henneman's size principle, and excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance. HD sEMG and kinematic data were collected from 23 healthy participants performing grasping tasks under different elbow and wrist postures. Performance was assessed using six prediction metrics and compared against six baseline machine learning and deep learning methods. The proposed method showed a large and significant ($p<0.05$, rank-biserial correlation $r_{rb}>0.7$) improvement over all baseline methods across all accuracy metrics. Performance improved significantly with increasing spike encoder firing rates up to approximately 128 Hz, and with more regular input spike trains compared with a Poisson-like encoder. In contrast, the E/I balance did not significantly affect the decoding performance of the algorithm. The firing rate and inter-spike interval statistics of the SNN differed significantly across motor tasks. These results demonstrate that incorporating neurophysiological principles into SNNs improves prediction performance while providing additional physiological interpretability for simultaneous and proportional finger-kinematics decoding. This approach represents a promising step toward physiology-informed neural networks, with potential applications in motor rehabilitation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a physiologically inspired spiking neural network (SNN) that decodes simultaneous, proportional, multi-joint finger kinematics from high-density surface electromyography (HD sEMG). Tested on 23 participants and compared with six conventional machine-learning/deep-learning baselines, the SNN significantly outperformed all baselines. Higher encoder firing rates and more regular spike trains improved performance, whereas excitation/inhibition balance had little measurable effect. The model also produced task-dependent neural activity patterns, supporting improved physiological interpretability.
AI.motivation: HD sEMG-based decoding of simultaneous and proportional finger movements is promising for applications such as motor rehabilitation, but existing data-driven models often lack physiological interpretability. The study is motivated by the need to combine strong decoding accuracy with biologically meaningful neural mechanisms. It therefore investigates whether incorporating spinal-inspired principles—noise variability, Henneman’s size principle, and excitation/inhibition balance—can improve or explain finger-kinematics prediction.
AI.method: The authors developed an SNN with spinal-inspired components: a spike-encoding model incorporating input-noise variability, a phenomenological implementation of Henneman’s size principle, and excitatory/inhibitory balance. HD sEMG and kinematic signals were recorded from 23 healthy participants performing grasping tasks under varied elbow and wrist postures. The model was evaluated using six prediction metrics and compared with six machine-learning and deep-learning baselines. Additional analyses examined the effects of encoder firing rate, spike-train regularity, E/I balance, and SNN firing-rate and inter-spike-interval statistics across tasks.
AI.result: The proposed SNN significantly outperformed all six baseline methods on every accuracy metric, with large effects (p<0.05; rank-biserial correlation >0.7). Decoding performance improved as spike-encoder firing rate increased to approximately 128 Hz. More regular spike trains performed better than Poisson-like spike trains. Changing E/I balance did not significantly affect prediction accuracy. SNN firing rates and inter-spike intervals varied significantly between motor tasks, indicating task-related internal dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Physiological principles embedded in an SNN can improve simultaneous and proportional finger-kinematics decoding from HD sEMG while offering greater interpretability than purely data-driven models. Encoder firing rate and spike-train regularity are important design factors, whereas E/I balance may be less influential under the tested conditions. The approach supports the development of physiology-informed neural networks for motor-rehabilitation technologies, although broader validation is needed to establish generalization across users and real-world settings.

title: Detecting and Understanding Ambiguity in Visualizations with Role-Playing Vision Language Model Interpretations
summary: Communicative visualizations can support multiple chart-grounded takeaways, including divergent or conflicting ones; we refer to this variation as interpretive ambiguity. Such ambiguity can undermine a visualization's communicative goal when the supported takeaways diverge from its intended message. Evaluating visualizations with target audiences can surface this variation, but such evaluations can be costly and difficult to scale. In this work, we explore persona-conditioned Vision Language Models (VLMs) as a complementary evaluation tool for interpretive ambiguity. For a given visualization, our pipeline uses topic-relevant personas to elicit candidate contextual takeaways supported by interpretations of perceived visual patterns, such as trends and clusters. We derive a Target--Pattern--Scope framework for comparing these interpretations, use LLM judges to assign Compatible, Disjoint, or Opposing ambiguity labels to statement pairs, and summarize their distribution in an ambiguity profile. To improve chart grounding, we benchmark candidate VLMs on chart comprehension and select the highest-performing model for each chart type. We evaluate statement-pair labeling against human-authored annotations and apply the approach to real-world, public-facing visualizations curated from established datasets. Through case studies, we examine how perceived visual patterns relate to contextual takeaways and how a visualization redesign changes the sampled interpretations. Our findings show how persona-conditioned VLMs can complement human feedback by generating candidate contextual takeaways and surfacing potential ambiguity for further inspection.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a scalable, complementary method for detecting interpretive ambiguity in communicative visualizations using persona-conditioned Vision Language Models (VLMs). The pipeline generates contextual takeaways, compares them through a Target–Pattern–Scope framework, labels statement-pair relationships, and summarizes ambiguity in profiles. Results suggest that VLMs can surface potentially divergent interpretations for human inspection, but they complement rather than replace audience-based evaluation.
AI.motivation: Visualizations may support multiple, divergent, or conflicting interpretations even when they have a specific intended message. This interpretive ambiguity can weaken communication, while conventional audience evaluations are expensive and difficult to scale. The paper therefore investigates whether persona-conditioned VLMs can provide an efficient preliminary or complementary evaluation mechanism.
AI.method: For each visualization, the pipeline uses topic-relevant personas to prompt VLMs to generate candidate contextual takeaways grounded in perceived visual patterns such as trends and clusters. Interpretations are organized using a Target–Pattern–Scope framework. LLM judges classify pairs of statements as Compatible, Disjoint, or Opposing, and the label distribution is summarized as an ambiguity profile. Candidate VLMs are benchmarked on chart-comprehension tasks, with the best-performing model selected for each chart type. The authors compare automated statement-pair labels with human annotations and analyze real-world visualizations from established datasets, including redesign case studies.
AI.result: The approach produces candidate contextual takeaways and ambiguity profiles that expose how visual patterns can lead to different contextual conclusions. Statement-pair labeling is evaluated against human-authored annotations, and case studies show that redesigns can alter the interpretations sampled by the system. Overall, the findings indicate that persona-conditioned VLMs are useful for surfacing potential ambiguity, provided that chart grounding and model selection are carefully addressed.
AI.conclusion: Persona-conditioned VLMs can serve as a scalable complement to human feedback in visualization evaluation. They help identify potentially compatible, disjoint, or opposing interpretations and support inspection of how design changes affect meaning. However, the method is best viewed as a screening and exploratory tool rather than a substitute for evaluation with real target audiences.

title: Perceived Acceptability of Sensory Augmentation
summary: Sensory augmentation (SA) can extend how people perceive and engage with public environments through the body, offering opportunities to support shared multimodal experiences between deaf and hearing visitors. Designing such systems requires understanding which combinations of tactile stimuli and body locations users perceive as acceptable. We examined the perceived acceptability of fictitious yet feasible SA configurations in a museum use-case. Using a modified technology acceptance model, we surveyed 307 deaf and hearing participants about tactile stimulus types and body locations. The results showed significant effects of stimulus type and body location on acceptance, but no interactions with hearing status. Participants generally preferred temperature-based stimuli, subtle movement, texture, and tickling over vibration, and distal over proximal body locations. These findings suggest that tactile SA design should be guided primarily by embodied and contextual factors rather than hearing status, informing future systems for shared multimodal experience in public cultural settings.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates which tactile stimuli and body locations are most acceptable for sensory augmentation (SA) systems intended to support shared museum experiences for deaf and hearing visitors. In a survey of 307 participants, acceptance depended on both stimulus type and body location, but not on hearing status or its interaction with these factors. Temperature, subtle movement, texture, and tickling were preferred to vibration, while distal body locations were preferred to proximal ones.
AI.motivation: Sensory augmentation can broaden how people experience public environments and may enable deaf and hearing visitors to participate in shared multimodal experiences. However, designing acceptable tactile interfaces requires evidence about which tactile sensations and body locations users are willing to have used, particularly in public cultural settings and across different hearing-status groups.
AI.method: The researchers examined a museum-related SA use case using a modified Technology Acceptance Model. They surveyed 307 deaf and hearing participants about the acceptability of fictitious but technically feasible configurations that varied in tactile stimulus type and body location. The analysis tested the main effects of stimulus type and location, as well as whether hearing status moderated these effects.
AI.result: Both tactile stimulus type and body location significantly influenced perceived acceptance. Participants generally preferred temperature-based stimulation, subtle movement, texture, and tickling over vibration, and preferred distal body locations over proximal locations. Hearing status did not significantly interact with either design factor, indicating broadly similar preference patterns among deaf and hearing participants.
AI.conclusion: Acceptable tactile SA for shared public experiences should be designed mainly around embodied and contextual considerations rather than hearing status. The findings provide initial guidance for selecting less intrusive tactile modalities and distal body locations in future museum and other public-cultural SA systems, although further evaluation with operational prototypes and real-world use is needed.

title: Toward Neuroadaptive Communication Interfaces: A Framework for Personalized Speech and Language Support
summary: Speech and language technologies have expanded access to communication, but the support they provide is often fixed. The same linguistic or visual aid may help one user and hinder another, or become less useful as task demands change. This project proposes a framework for adapting language presentation to individual abilities and ongoing interaction. It separates access to a message from the estimation of user needs and from the selection of support, including sentence segmentation, pictograms, and optional spoken output. Behavioral feedback provides the primary evidence for adaptation; electroencephalography is considered an additional, uncertainty-aware source of information rather than a direct measure of comprehension. We specify a staged evaluation comparing fixed, behavior-adaptive, and neuroadaptive interfaces. The central question is whether neural information improves comprehension and communication efficiency beyond a strong behavioral baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an adaptive language-presentation framework that personalizes supports such as sentence segmentation, pictograms, and speech using behavioral feedback, with EEG evaluated as an uncertainty-aware supplement. It compares fixed, behavior-adaptive, and neuroadaptive interfaces to determine whether neural information adds value beyond behavioral adaptation.
AI.motivation: Current speech and language aids are often static, even though users differ in ability and may need different support as task demands change. A support that benefits one user may hinder another, creating a need for adaptive systems. The paper is motivated by testing whether EEG can improve personalization and communication outcomes beyond behavioral signals alone.
AI.method: The framework separates three functions: delivering the message, estimating the user’s needs, and selecting the appropriate support. Candidate supports include sentence segmentation, pictograms, and optional spoken output. Behavioral interaction data are used as the primary adaptation signal, while EEG is treated as an additional, uncertainty-aware source rather than a direct comprehension measure. Evaluation is staged across three conditions: fixed interfaces, behavior-adaptive interfaces, and neuroadaptive interfaces.
AI.result: The abstract does not report empirical results. It defines the planned comparison and the central evaluation criterion: whether adding neural information improves comprehension and communication efficiency relative to a strong behavior-adaptive baseline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed work positions behavioral adaptation as the main practical baseline and EEG as a potentially useful but uncertain supplementary signal. Its contribution is a structured framework and staged evaluation for determining whether neuroadaptive language presentation provides measurable benefits over fixed and behavior-only systems.

title: Rewriting the Self: User Perceptions of AI-Mediated Cognitive Reframing
summary: Individuals are increasingly using AI for psychological support. One specific paradigm, AI-mediated cognitive reframing (AIM-CR), uses AI to automatically reframe users' negative thoughts ("I failed...") into more adaptive perspectives ("I am learning..."). While prior work suggests that AIM-CR tools reduce users' negative emotions, the complexities of AI automatically modifying users' personal narratives remain underexplored. In this work, we investigated these complexities through a mixed-methods study in which 28 participants engaged with an AIM-CR tool that reframed narratives about their stressors. Our findings suggest that participants had mixed perceptions of AIM-CR: although reframing reduced negative emotions for most participants, participants felt less ownership of, and less authenticity in, the reframed narratives. Participants perceived AIM-CR as a validating "mirror," as "another self" that could motivate or alienate them, or as an external social actor. These perceptions shaped therapeutic dynamics. We conclude by discussing design implications for future AIM-CR tools to better preserve user agency in narrative co-construction and more effectively support mental health and well-being.

AI.tldr: A mixed-methods study of 28 participants examines AI-mediated cognitive reframing (AIM-CR), finding that it often reduces negative emotions but can weaken users’ perceived ownership and authenticity of their personal narratives. The paper identifies three ways users perceive the AI—as a validating mirror, another self, or an external social actor—and derives design implications for preserving agency in therapeutic narrative co-construction.
AI.motivation: Existing research indicates that AI-mediated cognitive reframing can reduce negative emotions, but it has not sufficiently examined the psychological and relational consequences of AI automatically altering users’ personal narratives. The study addresses this gap by investigating how users experience ownership, authenticity, and therapeutic dynamics when AI reframes accounts of personal stressors.
AI.method: The researchers conducted a mixed-methods study with 28 participants. Participants interacted with an AI-mediated cognitive reframing tool that transformed negative narratives about their stressors into more adaptive perspectives. The study assessed emotional changes and explored participants’ subjective perceptions of the reframed narratives, including feelings of ownership, authenticity, validation, motivation, and alienation.
AI.result: AIM-CR reduced negative emotions for most participants, but participants also reported reduced ownership and authenticity in the AI-generated reframed narratives. They understood the AI in three main ways: as a validating mirror, as another self that could either motivate or alienate them, and as an external social actor. These interpretations influenced the therapeutic dynamics of the interaction.
AI.conclusion: AI reframing can provide emotional benefits while simultaneously creating tensions around agency, authenticity, and narrative ownership. Future AIM-CR systems should support user control and collaborative narrative construction rather than replacing users’ interpretations, thereby better balancing emotional support with personal authenticity and mental well-being.

title: The CAPED Framework: Characterizing User Skills in Chart Authoring through the Lens of Tasks and Tools
comment: Accepted at IEEE VIS 2026, to appear in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (TVCG)
summary: In this paper, we introduce a new framework for characterizing the user skills required for chart authoring. Despite growing attention to authoring systems, we lack a conceptual framework that characterizes the diverse and multifaceted skills involved and helps identify opportunities for system design and development. Our initial investigation revealed that skill is a complex and elusive concept, and that existing theories on skills from other disciplines are too high-level to capture the importance of tasks and tools in data visualizations. To address this gap, we formulate the CAPED framework that characterizes skill as the ability to create a chart involving five dimensions pertinent to tasks and tools: input data, output chart, paradigm, abstraction, and expression. We demonstrate the framework's descriptive power by highlighting different skills involved in similar authoring situations and identifying the types of knowledge associated with chart authoring. We further present examples illustrating how the framework can be used to identify new research opportunities in supporting users with varying skills.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CAPED, a five-dimensional framework for characterizing the skills required to author charts: input data, output chart, paradigm, abstraction, and expression. It uses the framework to distinguish authoring skills, organize related knowledge, and reveal opportunities for designing better authoring systems.
AI.motivation: Existing chart-authoring research lacks a conceptual framework for describing the diverse skills users need. General theories of skill are too abstract to represent the specific roles of tasks, tools, and visualization-authoring processes, limiting the ability to compare user capabilities and guide system development.
AI.method: The authors conduct an initial investigation of chart-authoring skill and synthesize its findings into the CAPED framework. CAPED characterizes skill as the ability to create a chart across five dimensions: input data, output chart, paradigm, abstraction, and expression. They demonstrate the framework through comparative examples of similar authoring situations and analyze the kinds of knowledge involved.
AI.result: The framework distinguishes different skills that may be required in superficially similar chart-authoring scenarios. It also categorizes associated knowledge and illustrates how CAPED can expose gaps and opportunities for supporting users with different skill profiles.
AI.conclusion: CAPED provides a task- and tool-sensitive vocabulary for understanding chart-authoring skill. The framework can help researchers and system designers reason about user abilities, compare authoring situations, and develop adaptive or more supportive visualization-authoring systems.

title: Affective and Functional Needs in AI Use: User Patterns and Their Relation to Real-Life Support and Well-Being
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, including supplementary material. Full paper accepted at the 14th International Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction (ACII 2026), forthcoming in IEEE Xplore
summary: Conversational AI systems are increasingly used to fulfill both functional and affective needs, yet how users perceive the AI-adoption effects varies. Existing research tends to treat these two needs as binary categories and to classify users by a single dominant need. However, this approach fails to capture users who engage with AI for both affective and functional purposes simultaneously, leaving it unclear how these needs combine in real-world AI use. To capture the multifaceted nature of users' AI engagement, we developed the AI-Support measurement with 1,090 participants, grounded in social support theory, which evaluates four dimensions of perceived AI support: emotional/esteem, social companionship, informational, and instrumental support. This study provided (1) an AI-Support Scale developed to measure the perceived support types from human-AI interaction, (2) evidence that users might adopt AI with a high level of both functional and affective use, and (3) exploratory indicators of users' real-life social support and well-being, enabling descriptive results aligning with theoretical expectations. Overall, this study highlights the importance of understanding individual differences in AI affordance use, enabling AI systems to be designed in alignment with different user adoption profiles rather than assuming uniform benefits across all users.

AI.tldr: The paper develops and evaluates a multidimensional AI-Support Scale, showing that users can simultaneously seek functional and affective support from conversational AI and that AI-use profiles may relate to social support and well-being.
AI.motivation: Existing studies often divide AI use into functional versus affective purposes and assign users to one dominant category. This binary, single-need approach overlooks people who use conversational AI for both purposes and does not adequately explain variation in perceived effects of AI adoption. The study therefore seeks a more nuanced framework grounded in social support theory.
AI.method: The authors developed an AI-Support measurement instrument using data from 1,090 participants. The instrument assesses four perceived support dimensions in human-AI interaction: emotional/esteem support, social companionship, informational support, and instrumental support. The study also examined exploratory associations between AI-support perceptions, participants' real-life social support, and well-being.
AI.result: The study produced an AI-Support Scale and found evidence that users may report high levels of both affective and functional AI use rather than belonging exclusively to one category. The exploratory findings concerning social support and well-being were descriptive and broadly consistent with theoretical expectations.
AI.conclusion: AI use should be understood as multidimensional and user-dependent rather than as uniformly functional or affective. Designing conversational AI around distinct user adoption profiles may better accommodate individual differences and avoid assuming that AI produces the same benefits for everyone.

title: Babysitting AI Agents: A User-Centered Taxonomy and Study of Agentic Delegation Failures
summary: Users are increasingly delegating tasks to AI agents, allowing agents to perform long-running, multi-step workflows on their behalf. However, agents may perform these tasks in ways that depart from users' expectations for how they should be carried out, leading to what we call agentic delegation failures. We leverage a large corpus of 163,487 Reddit posts, describing AI agent use, to develop MANDATE: a taxonomy of 23 failure categories organized into seven groups. A follow-up study with 73 AI agent users examined the relationship between prevalence and perceptions of severity and noticeability, finding that failures rated as more severe are considered harder to notice, and that prior experience with a failure is associated with greater noticeability. Finally, we assess the maturity of research on each failure and identify commonly encountered failures that have received little attention (e.g., agents running without making progress). Our findings inform opportunities to make delegation easier for users to oversee and better studied by the research community.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MANDATE, a taxonomy of agentic delegation failures derived from 163,487 Reddit posts and evaluated through a user study of 73 AI-agent users. It identifies 23 failure categories across seven groups, analyzes their prevalence, severity, and noticeability, and highlights under-researched but common failures.
AI.motivation: As AI agents increasingly execute long-running, multi-step tasks for users, they may complete tasks in ways that violate users’ expectations even when the overall objective is pursued. Existing research lacks a systematic account of these delegation failures, especially failures that are difficult for users to detect or oversee. The paper aims to organize these failure modes, understand how users perceive them, and identify gaps in current research.
AI.method: The authors first analyzed a large corpus of 163,487 Reddit posts describing AI-agent use to construct MANDATE, a taxonomy containing 23 failure categories grouped into seven higher-level groups. They then conducted a follow-up study with 73 AI-agent users to examine perceived severity, noticeability, prevalence, and the relationship between prior experience and detection. Finally, they assessed the maturity of existing research coverage for each failure category.
AI.result: The taxonomy provides a structured overview of agentic delegation failures. The user study found that failures perceived as more severe tend to be harder to notice, creating a risk that consequential problems remain undetected. Users with prior experience of a given failure tend to perceive it as more noticeable. The research-maturity analysis revealed that several common failures have received limited scholarly attention, including agents continuing to run without making progress.
AI.conclusion: MANDATE offers a foundation for studying and designing against failures that arise when users delegate complex workflows to AI agents. The findings suggest that oversight mechanisms should prioritize severe but difficult-to-detect failures, while researchers should address underexplored failure modes that occur frequently in practice. Overall, the paper supports safer, more transparent, and more manageable delegation to AI agents.

title: The Impact of Personalized AI Response Suggestions on Content Creators' Direct Messaging
summary: Direct messaging is often employed by social media content creators to directly interact with followers. Those creators attempt to engage with followers in private communication, but they often encounter a large volume of messages. Through formative interviews with 15 creators, we found that creators frequently experience fatigue from writing suitable content, as they moderate audience expectations while concurrently integrating their media personas into responses. To explore how AI can address these challenges, we designed a system providing personalized, AI-generated response suggestions tailored to creators' writing styles to maintain their media personas. In a comparison study with 13 creators that examines how the system affects response behaviors, creators valued the system's ability to soften potential impoliteness and anticipated higher response rates, helping them maintain a professional image. However, creators reported additional labor in verifying the authenticity of AI outputs to mitigate risks caused by AI misalignment. Our results indicate that while AI suggestions enhance efficiency, they can undermine a creator's engagement in communication by shifting their attention toward monitoring AI.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates personalized AI-generated direct-message response suggestions for social media creators. The system may improve efficiency, politeness, response rates, and professional self-presentation, but it also creates verification work and redirects creators’ attention from followers to monitoring AI outputs.
AI.motivation: Social media creators receive many direct messages and must craft responses that satisfy audience expectations while preserving their media personas. This causes writing fatigue and creates a need for tools that reduce effort without compromising authenticity, appropriateness, or professional image.
AI.method: The researchers conducted formative interviews with 15 creators to understand messaging challenges, then designed a system that generates personalized response suggestions based on creators’ writing styles. They evaluated the system in a comparison study with 13 creators, examining changes in response behavior and creators’ perceptions of the system.
AI.result: Creators appreciated the system’s ability to reduce writing effort, soften potentially impolite wording, support anticipated increases in response rates, and help maintain a professional image. However, they needed to verify whether AI-generated responses were authentic and properly aligned with their persona, which introduced additional labor and concerns about AI misalignment.
AI.conclusion: Personalized AI suggestions can improve the efficiency and social appropriateness of creator–follower communication, but their benefits are not unconditionally positive. By requiring creators to monitor and authenticate AI outputs, the system may shift attention away from interpersonal engagement and partially undermine the very communication it is intended to support.

title: ECHOES: An Adaptive LLM-Powered AR Glasses Docent for Evidence-Grounded Urban Heritage Interpretation
summary: Urban heritage tours are often delivered through fixed scripts, leaving limited room for visitors' situated questions, language preferences, or requests for evidence. We present ECHOES, an adaptive LLM-powered AR glasses docent for evidence-grounded interpretation of historical buildings. Specifically, the agent adapts along three dimensions: it modifies response structure according to the type of visitor question (identification, architectural detail, evidence-seeking, or route inquiry); it accumulates session-level interest signals from repeated questions and expressed curiosity to shape later explanations; and it tracks language preference and retrieval context across turns to maintain conversational continuity. The core of ECHOES is an LLM agent initialized as a source-aware urban heritage docent that realizes this adaptation through dialogue and preference context maintained across the session. Around this agent, ECHOES integrates visual site grounding, a self-built historical knowledge base supporting retrieval-augmented generation, and concise multilingual AR output designed for glanceable use. Through a working prototype centered on Shanghai's East Nanjing Road and the Bund, we demonstrate how an adaptive LLM-powered AR docent can transform historical tours from scripted narration into situated, question-responsive, and source-aware conversations.

AI.tldr: ECHOES is a prototype adaptive LLM-powered AR glasses docent that uses visual grounding, a historical knowledge base, retrieval-augmented generation, and session context to provide concise, multilingual, evidence-aware responses during urban heritage tours. It adapts to question type, visitor interests, language preferences, and retrieval context, demonstrated through a case study of Shanghai’s East Nanjing Road and the Bund.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the limitations of fixed-script urban heritage tours, which cannot adequately respond to situated visitor questions, evolving interests, language preferences, or requests for historical evidence. The goal is to make heritage interpretation more interactive, personalized, context-aware, and source-grounded while remaining suitable for glanceable AR use.
AI.method: The authors develop ECHOES, an LLM-based conversational AR docent. Its adaptation operates across three dimensions: response structure is tailored to question categories; repeated questions and expressed curiosity create session-level interest signals; and language preference plus retrieval context are maintained across turns. The system combines a source-aware LLM agent with visual site grounding, a self-built historical knowledge base, retrieval-augmented generation, and concise multilingual AR presentation. A working prototype is deployed for heritage sites around Shanghai’s East Nanjing Road and the Bund.
AI.result: The prototype demonstrates that ECHOES can provide question-responsive, interest-adaptive, multilingual, and evidence-oriented interpretation of historical buildings in an AR setting. It shows how conversational context and retrieval support can transform a tour from scripted narration into situated dialogue. However, the abstract reports a demonstration rather than quantitative evaluation, so effectiveness, factuality, usability, and visitor learning gains are not established in detail.
AI.conclusion: ECHOES illustrates the feasibility of an adaptive, source-aware LLM AR docent for urban heritage interpretation. By combining visual grounding, historical retrieval, and session-level personalization, it offers a promising alternative to fixed-script tours, although broader user studies and systematic evaluation are needed to validate its reliability and impact.

title: Visible Reasoning: User-Facing Decision Transparency for Generative AI Systems
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures. Original pre-review author manuscript; LaTeX source reconstructed from the author's PDF. Published version: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-30849-8_1
summary:
Across multiple waves of computing, public trust in new technology has followed the emergence of governance mechanisms that made dominant risks legible and manageable. Generative AI shifts this pattern: these systems synthesize across heterogeneous sources, and users increasingly experience them as reasoning systems. The central question changes from "did it perform correctly?" to "can we trust how it arrived at its conclusion?"
  This paper introduces Filtered Decision Logs (FDLs), a user-facing transparency mechanism that makes decision formation visible without exposing raw chain-of-thought. FDLs pair each response with (i) a concise decision rationale, (ii) influence-ordered supporting data points derived from tool outputs, and (iii) relevance indicators showing which sources most shaped the conclusion. To operationalize evidence selection, we propose a trace-based method that reconstructs observability telemetry into a provenance tree and ranks evidence using four deterministic semantic and structural signals - Final Answer Similarity, Average Relevancy, Persistence, and Structural Proximity - combined via adaptive weighted scoring. We demonstrate FDLs across three domains: career advising (5 tools), investment analysis (4 tools), and travel planning (4 tools). In a formative evaluation with 50 participants (25 students, 25 working professionals in AI development), 92% rated the influence-ranked evidence as helpful for understanding and trusting the system's recommendation. Counterfactual tool-removal experiments confirm that removing the top-ranked source changes the answer more than removing a low-ranked source, validating that the ranking tracks decision dependence. We conclude that evidence-ranked transparency helps users identify misleading signals and missing context, enabling more confident acceptance, correction, or re-run of system decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Filtered Decision Logs (FDLs), a transparent interface for generative-AI decisions that exposes concise rationales and influence-ranked evidence without revealing raw chain-of-thought. A provenance-tree method ranks evidence using four deterministic signals, and evaluations suggest the rankings improve users’ understanding and track decision dependence.
AI.motivation: Generative AI increasingly appears to users as a reasoning system, making conventional outcome-based evaluation insufficient for trust. Users need to understand how evidence contributed to a conclusion while avoiding disclosure of private or unsafe raw chain-of-thought. The paper addresses this transparency and trust gap.
AI.method: FDLs attach three elements to each response: a concise decision rationale, influence-ordered supporting data points from tool outputs, and source-relevance indicators. The system reconstructs observability telemetry into a provenance tree and ranks evidence using Final Answer Similarity, Average Relevancy, Persistence, and Structural Proximity, combined through adaptive weighted scoring. It is demonstrated in career advising, investment analysis, and travel planning. A formative study with 50 participants evaluates perceived helpfulness, while counterfactual tool-removal experiments test whether rankings reflect decision dependence.
AI.result: Across the three application domains, 92% of participants reported that influence-ranked evidence helped them understand and trust recommendations. Removing the highest-ranked source changed the answer more than removing a low-ranked source, providing evidence that the ranking captures the relative contribution of sources to decisions.
AI.conclusion: Evidence-ranked transparency can make generative-AI decision formation more legible without exposing raw chain-of-thought. FDLs may help users detect misleading evidence and missing context and make more informed decisions to accept, correct, or rerun system outputs. The findings support provenance-based transparency as a practical trust mechanism for tool-using AI systems.

title: Beyond Being Accurate: Implications for Using Natural Language Descriptions for Accessible 3D Modeling with~Blind and Low Vision Makers
summary: People who are blind or have low vision (BLV) are largely excluded from 3D modeling tools that rely on visual representations of geometry. Natural language descriptions offer a potential path to accessibility, but it is unclear whether language alone can support the deep spatial understanding that editing, not just browsing, requires. Advances in generative AI offer the promise of automatic model description, yet descriptions suited to BLV modelers are structurally distinct from alt-text and from existing 3D model captioning datasets, and the domain-specific requirements for generating them are not well understood. We address this through two coordinated studies: an autoethnographic pilot in which the blind first author worked with 12 sighted participants to develop a taxonomy of descriptive strategies, and a Wizard-of-Oz main study that applied those strategies as idealized scripts with 10 BLV participants. We identify a systematic use-to-editing gap: descriptions that support accurate but incomplete mental models are insufficient for specifying modifications, because editing requires knowing the state of features the user did not know to ask about. We show that this gap produces four failure types (accuracy, completeness, expression, and navigation) that accuracy-focused evaluation frameworks cannot detect. We propose a two-phase evaluation framework that diagnoses the failure type a description system exhibits and guides developers toward targeted design interventions, thereby providing a methodological standard for assessing whether description-based systems genuinely support BLV modelers as creators.

AI.tldr: The paper examines whether natural-language descriptions can make 3D modeling accessible to people who are blind or have low vision (BLV). Through an autoethnographic pilot and a Wizard-of-Oz study, it identifies a use-to-editing gap: descriptions may support an approximate mental model for understanding a 3D object but still omit information needed to modify it. The paper categorizes four failure types—accuracy, completeness, expression, and navigation—and proposes a two-phase evaluation framework for diagnosing and improving description-based modeling systems.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D modeling tools depend heavily on visual geometry representations, excluding BLV users. Although natural language and generative AI could improve accessibility, descriptions for editing 3D models have different structural and domain-specific requirements than alt-text or conventional 3D captions. The paper therefore investigates what information BLV modelers need and how description systems should be evaluated beyond simple factual accuracy.
AI.method: The research used two coordinated qualitative studies. First, an autoethnographic pilot involved the blind first author and 12 sighted participants to develop a taxonomy of descriptive strategies. Second, a Wizard-of-Oz study used idealized descriptions based on that taxonomy with 10 BLV participants. The authors analyzed how descriptions supported model understanding, modification specification, and interaction/navigation, then derived recurring failure categories and an evaluation framework.
AI.result: The studies revealed a systematic gap between using descriptions to understand or browse a model and using them to edit it. Participants could form accurate but incomplete mental models, yet lacked information about unrequested or unseen feature states that was necessary for specifying changes. Four failure types were identified: accuracy failures, completeness failures, expression failures, and navigation failures. The findings show that accuracy-oriented evaluation alone misses important barriers to effective editing.
AI.conclusion: Natural-language 3D descriptions should be evaluated as tools for creation and editing, not merely as captions or browsing aids. The proposed two-phase framework first diagnoses which failure type occurs and then directs targeted design interventions. This provides a methodological basis for developing description systems that genuinely support BLV users as 3D modelers.

title: Reflective Computing
summary: Interactive technology is increasingly built for speed, and generative AI now answers before a question is fully formed. Yet the capacity to pause, interpret and decide for oneself is central to wellbeing, learning and meaningful use. HCI has named paradigms for sensing emotion, changing behavior, calming attention and tracking the self. However, none of them takes human reflection, and the slowing down it requires, as its organizing aim. This article defines that paradigm, reflective computing, and derives it from what thirty years of designs lack. We analyzed 134 interactive systems from 17 ACM venues (1996-2026) in two phases. First, an abductive gap analysis read every system against reflection theory, and seven recurring gaps defined seven dimensions, namely tempo agency, invitational form, interpretive openness, reflective depth, temporal span, protected idleness and ethical non-extraction. Second, two independent coders scored every system with a codebook (Krippendorff's alpha 0.67 to 0.84 for five dimensions; ICC 0.82 for the overall score). The system sets the pace in 51 designs, 74 support only momentary use, only 12 scaffold reflection beyond description, and 56 papers are silent on the inner states they collect. No system expresses all seven dimensions strongly, and only 20 meet the definition. Slow and experience centered design comes closest, whereas persuasive technology and human-AI interaction score lowest. Factor and latent class analyses reveal two cultures of reflection, one working through form and the other through scaffolded thought, which only one system combines. Systems that let people set the pace score markedly higher, even with paradigm and form controlled (odds ratio 13.5). Hence, reflective computing is proposed as a paradigm whose aim is a human capacity rather than a system function, and which treats slowness as valuable only when people choose it.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes reflective computing as an HCI paradigm centered on enabling human reflection rather than optimizing speed, persuasion, emotion regulation, or self-tracking. An analysis of 134 systems identifies seven design dimensions and finds that most systems offer limited, system-controlled support for reflection; user control over pacing is strongly associated with stronger reflective qualities.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by the increasing speed and proactivity of interactive and generative-AI systems, which may reduce users’ opportunities to pause, interpret experiences, and make independent decisions. Although HCI has developed paradigms addressing emotion, behavior, attention, and self-tracking, the authors argue that reflection—and the deliberate slowing it may require—has not been established as the primary design objective. The study therefore seeks to define reflective computing and identify how prior systems fail to support it.
AI.method: The authors conducted a two-phase analysis of 134 interactive systems published across 17 ACM venues from 1996 to 2026. In phase one, they used abductive gap analysis, interpreting each system through reflection theory and deriving seven recurring dimensions: tempo agency, invitational form, interpretive openness, reflective depth, temporal span, protected idleness, and ethical non-extraction. In phase two, two independent coders applied a codebook to all systems. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using Krippendorff’s alpha for five dimensions and ICC for the overall score. The authors also used factor analysis and latent class analysis to identify broader patterns, and logistic modeling to examine the relationship between user control over pacing and reflective quality while controlling for paradigm and form.
AI.result: The findings show substantial weaknesses in existing systems. In only 51 designs did the system set the pace in a way that supported reflection, 74 supported only momentary engagement, and just 12 scaffolded reflection beyond simple description. Fifty-six papers did not address the inner states they collected, raising ethical concerns about non-extraction. No system strongly expressed all seven dimensions, and only 20 satisfied the proposed definition of reflective computing. Slow and experience-centered design came closest to the paradigm, while persuasive technology and human–AI interaction scored lowest. Factor and latent-class analyses identified two reflection cultures: one emphasizing form and another emphasizing scaffolded thought; only one system combined both. Systems giving users control over pace were substantially more likely to achieve stronger reflective qualities, with an odds ratio of 13.5 after controlling for paradigm and form.
AI.conclusion: The paper proposes reflective computing as a distinct HCI paradigm whose primary goal is to cultivate a human capacity—reflection—rather than provide a narrow system function. It argues that slowness is not inherently beneficial: it becomes valuable when users can choose the pace and when designs support interpretation, depth, temporal continuity, protected idleness, and ethical handling of inner-state data. The empirical results support user-controlled pacing as a particularly important design principle, while also showing that current systems rarely integrate the full set of reflective qualities.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
summary: Visual search is ubiquitous in daily life, from locating keys in a messy apartment to finding a tool in a cluttered workshop or an application icon on a desktop screen. While visual attention is to a large extent driven by image content, research in psychology indicates that user cognitive states have a significant influence on attention allocation. A promising way to access information about cognitive states is via Electroencephalography (EEG) recordings. Despite this potential, previous works in computational attention modeling have largely disregarded EEG, and related studies in psychology operate with abstract, simplistic stimuli, or even artificially guided search procedures. We bridge this gap with two contributions. First, we present EEGaze 140, the largest publicly available multimodal dataset of free visual search with realistic stimuli. The dataset contains synchronized EEG and eye tracking recordings from 36 participants across 140 naturalistic scenes, covering two scenarios: searching for desktop icons and finding tools in cluttered workshop scenes. Second, we introduce EEGazeNet, the first method for human attention prediction in visual search that integrates EEG signals. Our approach consists of a EEG guided refinement stage that adapts the output of a state of the art saliency prediction method to the user current cognitive state. In comprehensive evaluations on EEGaze 140, we show that EEGazeNet consistently outperforms all baselines and ablation conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EEGaze 140, a large multimodal dataset combining EEG and eye tracking during realistic free visual-search tasks, and EEGazeNet, an EEG-guided attention-prediction model. EEGazeNet adapts image-based saliency predictions to a viewer’s current cognitive state and consistently outperforms comparison methods.
AI.motivation: Existing computational visual-attention models primarily rely on image content and largely ignore the observer’s cognitive state. Meanwhile, psychological studies using EEG often employ abstract stimuli or constrained search procedures that do not reflect natural visual search. The paper addresses this gap by collecting realistic multimodal data and developing a model that uses EEG to improve human attention prediction.
AI.method: The authors construct EEGaze 140, containing synchronized EEG and eye-tracking recordings from 36 participants viewing 140 naturalistic scenes in two tasks: finding desktop icons and locating tools in cluttered workshops. They then propose EEGazeNet, which combines a state-of-the-art saliency predictor with an EEG-guided refinement stage that adjusts predicted attention according to the user’s current cognitive state. Performance is evaluated against baseline models and ablation variants.
AI.result: On the EEGaze 140 benchmark, EEGazeNet consistently outperforms all evaluated baselines and ablation conditions, demonstrating that EEG provides useful information beyond visual content for predicting attention during visual search.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that cognitive-state information captured by EEG can improve attention prediction in realistic visual-search settings. EEGaze 140 enables further research on multimodal human-attention modeling, while EEGazeNet establishes an effective approach for integrating neural signals with saliency prediction.

title: The Evolution and 'Chineseness' of Urban Screens in China: From Propaganda Posters to Smart City Interfaces
comment: 14 pages. Accepted at the Media Architecture Biennale 2025 (MAB25), Bangkok
summary: Urban screens have become a global feature of the media city, yet their developmental paths are not universal. This paper argues that the evolution of urban screens in China constitutes a distinct paradigm of media urbanism, termed Chineseness, understood here not as cultural essence but as a relational, historically situated configuration of three linked elements: deep-rooted lineages of public communication; state-steered technological leapfrogging driven by industrial policy and mega-events; and a regulatory paradox that enables spectacular scale while tightening operational control. Drawing on a five-stage genealogy (1990-present), a chronology of representative screens, and five paradigmatic cases, the study shows how this configuration produces temporal-spatial compression, the coexistence of multiple technological generations, and privileges collective witnessing over device-centric interactivity. The paper contributes a documented genealogy of Chinese urban screens, develops temporal-spatial compression and collective witnessing as analytical tools for non-Western media ecologies, and positions Chineseness as a globally relevant alternative to market-led models of media architecture.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes “Chineseness” as a historically situated model of urban-screen development in China, explaining how public-communication traditions, state-led technological expansion, and paradoxical regulation generate a distinctive form of media urbanism.
AI.motivation: The study addresses the assumption that urban screens follow a universal or primarily market-led development path. It seeks to document China’s specific historical trajectory and provide analytical concepts that can support comparison with non-Western media ecologies.
AI.method: The paper uses a five-stage genealogy from 1990 to the present, a chronology of representative urban screens, and analysis of five paradigmatic cases. It synthesizes these materials through three dimensions: public-communication lineages, state-steered technological leapfrogging associated with industrial policy and mega-events, and regulation that combines spectacular expansion with tighter operational control.
AI.result: The analysis identifies three major outcomes: temporal-spatial compression, the coexistence of multiple technological generations, and a preference for collective witnessing over device-centered interactivity. Together, these outcomes distinguish China’s urban-screen ecology from market-led models of media architecture.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that “Chineseness” should be understood relationally and historically rather than as a cultural essence. It contributes a documented genealogy of Chinese urban screens and proposes temporal-spatial compression and collective witnessing as concepts for analyzing non-Western media urbanism, presenting China as a globally relevant alternative paradigm.
